children: Beth Hammack, president of the Cleveland Fed, sees "a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2% inflation," she said on Monday. However, she views financial conditions as neutral. That implies adjustments to tighten policy will be needed.

"When feasible, I generally think it’s preferable to make smaller adjustments and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction," she said at the National Association of Business Economists Annual Meeting in Cleveland.

In her assessment of the economy, she sees inflation pressures as "relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component," she said, according to her prepared text. Energy price increases have dominated headlines, but factors, including higher tariff rates and increasing demand from the AI buildout, are also contributing.
"Because of the breadth of inflationary pressures, my baseline forecast is that it will take some time for inflation to return to 2%, even with appropriate monetary policy," she said.

Hammack also emphasized why it's important that the public understand her "reaction function," or how she thinks policy is likely to unfold and how that may change by circumstance. "Explaining my reaction function is not a prediction for policy. It’s describing how I expect policy to adjust as conditions change," she said.
"Transparency has the benefit of allowing consumers, businesses, and financial markets to make better-informed decisions," Hammack added.

It's also important to distinguish between “reaction function” and “forward guidance”; the two terms shouldn't be used interchangeably. "Forward guidance is a specific tool: an explicit commitment about the future path of policy, typically deployed when the federal funds rate is at the effective lower bound, like it was following the financial crisis," she said.
"I think we need to get to a restrictive policy," Hammack said. "The question is over what timeframe."
"I want to cool the economy at the margins," she said, adding that she still hopes to keep the economy strong. Rather, "inflation that's been persistently too high" needs to come under control.
: Medium- and long-term inflation expectations are "reasonably well-anchored," but short-term inflation expectations have risen, Hammack said.

: With Fed Chair Kevin Warsh rethinking the central bank's communications, Hammack said she would miss it if the Fed stopped issuing the so-called “dot plot” in its Summary of Economic Projections. The dots indicate where the Federal Open Market Committee members expect the Fed's policy rate to go over time.
"I do think there's real information in the dot plot," she explained. "I would like to see a connected reaction function," meaning which dot is connected with other projections.

title: Cleveland Fed's Hammack sees restrictive policy as appropriate
